description: We're excited to take part in NASA Space Apps, challenge ourselves, and apply our skills to something that matters.
summary:
How can we protect wetlands when we cannot always see them?
BogSignal combines NASA–ISRO’s NISAR radar, Sentinel satellite imagery and machine learning to map wetlands in Polissia — a vast landscape known as Europe’s Amazon — and explore seasonal changes. Decades of drainage and land conversion have threatened these ecosystems, making conservation and restoration increasingly important.
We tested whether NISAR’s L-band radar improves wetland mapping beyond Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2. Against imperfect historical references, adding NISAR increased wetland overlap from 20.0% to 27.8% and recall from 32.5% to 39.6%. The highest-scoring 5% of our validation area contained 73.4% of reference Swamp and Marsh pixels, suggesting a way to prioritize field investigations.
Our interactive application lets visitors explore satellite imagery, compare predictions with and without NISAR, and investigate seasonal differences. A June–October comparison at three Ukrainian wetland sites illustrates the potential for broader monitoring, although prediction changes are not independently verified environmental changes.
We also published an open Kaggle dataset containing 3,753 aligned multisensor satellite patches to support further research.
BogSignal demonstrates how radar can improve wetland investigation and lay the groundwork for future monitoring.
details:
BogSignal is an interactive application combining NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations, machine learning and environmental data to map wetlands and explore seasonal changes.

Our study area is Polissia, one of Europe's largest wetland landscapes, spanning Ukraine, Poland, Belarus and Russia. Decades of drainage, agriculture and infrastructure development have transformed parts of the region, while conservation initiatives are working to restore its wetlands.

Our goal is to help researchers identify wetlands that conventional satellite imagery may miss, prioritize areas for investigation and explore environmental changes over time.

How it works

We developed a geospatial processing and machine-learning pipeline combining three satellite missions:

  • Sentinel-2: Optical imagery revealing vegetation, open water and land cover, but limited by clouds and dense canopies.
  • Sentinel-1: C-band radar (~5.6 cm wavelength), using VV and VH polarizations to capture surface moisture, roughness and vegetation structure.
  • NISAR: L-band radar (~24 cm wavelength), using HH and HV polarizations to provide additional information about vegetation and potentially concealed inundation.

Our approach combines two radar frequencies, four polarization channels and ascending and descending satellite observations. Historical wetland inventories, peatland maps, land-cover datasets and OpenStreetMap data provide provisional training labels.

Using a U-Net segmentation model with a ResNet-34 encoder, we predict six classes: Swamp, Marsh, Water, Peatland cropland, Peatland non-cropland and Other.

These categories reflect combined reference datasets rather than independently verified ecological conditions. In particular, peatland classifications do not establish degradation or restoration suitability.

What difference does NISAR make?

To measure NISAR's contribution, we trained four versions of the same model: Sentinel-2 alone, Sentinel-2 with Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 with NISAR, and all three satellites together. For wetland evaluation, we combine Swamp and Marsh into one category.

Adding NISAR improved agreement with historical wetland references: overlap (IoU) increased from 20.0% to 27.8%, while recall rose from 32.5% to 39.6%, compared with Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-1 alone.The same location: historical reference labels (left), predictions without NISAR (center), and predictions with NISAR (right). Green represents Swamp/Marsh; blue represents Water. The overall improvements were measured across the full validation area, not this individual example.

Beyond mapping, BogSignal could help researchers decide where to investigate first. The highest-scoring 5% of the validation area contained 73.4% of reference Swamp and Marsh pixels, suggesting a way to focus imagery review and field surveys. These results measure agreement with historical and inferred references, not independently verified wetland detection accuracy.

Interactive exploration and seasonal monitoring

We turned our findings into an interactive web application where visitors can:

  • Explore wetland predictions across approximately 133,000 km² of Polissia.
  • Compare optical, C-band and L-band satellite observations.
  • See NISAR's contribution using a slider comparing predictions with and without NISAR.
  • Investigate successes and limitations through selected examples.
  • Explore seasonal differences in satellite observations and model predictions.

To illustrate the potential for monitoring, we implemented a June–October 2026 comparison at three Ukrainian wetland sites: Cheremske, Somyne and Syra Pohonia.

Using the same trained model, we processed date-specific observations from all three satellites on matching spatial grids. Visitors can compare imagery, predicted wetland classes and maps highlighting where Swamp/Marsh predictions changed.

This exploratory demonstration illustrates a possible approach to broader wetland monitoring. However, changes in model predictions are not necessarily environmental changes. The comparison uses provisional NISAR observations and has not been independently validated.

Technologies and resources

BogSignal uses Python, PyTorch, geospatial raster-processing tools, Google Earth Engine, NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) data archive, and JavaScript with Leaflet.

Our pipeline handles satellite data discovery, acquisition, preprocessing, geographic alignment and model inference. Sentinel and NISAR observations are aligned to a common 20-meter grid.

We also experimented with averaging multiple NISAR observations to investigate whether repeated radar acquisitions improve wetland classification.

Open data & reproducibility

We published a companion research dataset to make BogSignal's work accessible and reusable.

Polissia Wetlands: NISAR and Sentinel-1/2, available on Kaggle, contains 3,753 aligned satellite patches with 14 input channels, validity masks, source metadata and a Python loader.

The imagery-only release includes guidance for reconstructing reference labels from their original sources. Segmentation labels are not distributed, and the underlying references remain historical and provisional.

This public dataset supports independent experimentation and further research, although reproducing our results and validating them against field observations require additional work.

Innovation and intended impact

BogSignal goes beyond displaying satellite imagery: it measures NISAR's contribution to wetland mapping and translates the findings into an accessible interactive application.

By integrating optical imagery with C-band and L-band radar, we investigate how complementary satellite observations can reveal wetland characteristics that individual sensors may miss. Our project delivers a comparative machine-learning experiment, an interactive exploration and seasonal-comparison application, and an openly published satellite dataset. The current results come from a single experimental run evaluated against provisional references, without an independent test set or field validation.

Future development will focus on independent validation, longer observation series and integrating historical drainage and hydrological evidence to investigate wetland change and restoration opportunities.

We cannot protect what we cannot see. BogSignal aims to help us see more — and know where to look next.
